newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Digital gains from Asian strategy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Digital gains from Asian strategy.

text.p: A "borderless" strategy in Southeast Asia has boosted Digital Equipment's performance and improved its inventories, senior company official J. Graham Long said on Thursday.

"The approach we've developed about a year and a half ago was to go after this territory in a borderless fashion. The growth has improved considerably," said Long, vice president for the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) region.
The "borderless" programme means Digital's partners in Southeast Asia and developing countries like Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh pay the same price for products.
The contracts they sign with Digital are also valid in all the countries, Long told Reuters in an interview.
He said it also meant Digital could also support its partners' programmes across borders. ASEAN comprises Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines, Brunei and Vietnam.
"Our overall business revenue grew 40 percent to US$400 million," for the financial year ended June 1996, Long said.
"For two years, we had flat growth in workstations. We implemented this strategy and then we grew 250 percent year to year. This year, we're going to double this business," he said.
The company's Alpha range of products grew 55 percent.

Long said Digital was aiming to increase revenues by 30 percent a year in the region for the next three years and to improve profits by 50 percent this fiscal year. He declined to give profit figures.
Orders for the first quarter ending this month were expected to be better than the same period last year, compared to a weaker quarter expected by Digital on a worldwide basis, he said.

Long said the "borderless" strategy was unique to Digital's Southeast Asian business and began when the company saw its partners, selling hardware or software, were expanding geographically as ASEAN moved towards eliminating intra-regional trade tariffs.
Digital's inventories in the region have also been cut.
"Now we're carrying one-third less inventory than we have before, compared to 18 months ago and we've gotten rid of redundant inventory," said Long.
Digital has centralised stocks at its Singapore plant and closed down warehouses in other ASEAN countries. It is now working on developing a central order desk out of Singapore, Long said.
He said competitors could adopt a similar strategy, but saw Digital with an edge from being the first to do it.
"The competition would have to break down barriers that took us one and half years to break," he said.

"Actually, we would encourage any vendor of size to implement a borderless strategy. We would lose some competitive advantage, but it would be good for the industry. It would be one way to bring IT solutions to developing countries faster."
Digital would focus on three areas of business in the region -- high-end Unix systems, Windows NT technology and Internet/Intranet business.

Its strong performance in the region has captured attention at group level, Long said. There was now greater pressure to keep doing better to help bolster the company's earnings on a worldwide basis, he said.
For fiscal year 1995/96, Digital reported a loss of US$111.8 million on a worldwide basis.
